\chapter{Boolean Analysis — Switching}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.BooleanAnalysis.Switching
\section{Overview}

This module assembles Håstad's Switching Lemma. Building on the Razborov-style
encoder and the canonical decision tree, it develops the combinatorial machinery
needed to count the restrictions $\rho$ under which a width-$w$ DNF $f$ restricts
to a function of large decision-tree depth, proves the path-consumption and
free-variable invariants of the encoder, and concludes both the DNF and (by De
Morgan duality) the CNF versions of the switching lemma together with their
representation-size corollaries.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Parse an aux list into triples]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux}
\leanok
Parses a low-level aux list of $(\mathbb{N} \times \mathrm{Bool})$ entries into
a list of triples $(\mathrm{pos}, \mathrm{dir}, \mathrm{hasMarker})$ with
$\mathrm{pos} : \mathrm{Fin}\,w$, where $\mathrm{hasMarker}$ records whether the
entry is immediately followed by a $(w, \mathrm{false})$ termination marker.
Entries with index $\geq w$ that do not follow a real entry are dropped.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Triples back to an aux list]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.triplesToAux}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.triplesToAux}
\leanok
The inverse direction of \texttt{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux}: converts a list of
triples back into an aux list of $(\mathbb{N} \times \mathrm{Bool})$ entries,
emitting a $(w, \mathrm{false})$ termination marker after each triple whose
marker flag is true.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Parsing an entry immediately followed by a termination marker]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_cons_marker}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_cons_marker}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux}
\difficulty{2}
Fix a width $w \ge 1$ and an index $\mathrm{idx} < w$, together with a direction bit
$\mathrm{dir}$ and an arbitrary list of remaining entries $\mathrm{rest}$. Parsing the
list that begins with the entry $(\mathrm{idx}, \mathrm{dir})$, followed immediately by
the termination marker $(w, \mathrm{false})$, and then by $\mathrm{rest}$, produces the
triple $(\mathrm{idx}, \mathrm{dir}, \mathrm{true})$ — with $\mathrm{idx}$ viewed as an
element of $\{0, \dots, w-1\}$ and the final component recording that this entry is
marked — prepended to the parse of $\mathrm{rest}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Parsing an entry followed by an in-range entry]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_cons_nonmarker}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_cons_nonmarker}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux}
\difficulty{2}
Fix $w \geq 1$, and consider parsing an aux list whose first two entries are
$(\mathrm{idx}, \mathrm{dir})$ and $(\mathrm{idx}', \mathrm{dir}')$, both with in-range
indices $\mathrm{idx} < w$ and $\mathrm{idx}' < w$, followed by any further list
$\mathrm{rest}$. Then parsing $(\mathrm{idx}, \mathrm{dir}) :: (\mathrm{idx}',
\mathrm{dir}') :: \mathrm{rest}$ yields the triple $(\mathrm{idx}, \mathrm{dir},
\mathrm{false})$ — with no termination marker recorded — prepended to the parse of
$(\mathrm{idx}', \mathrm{dir}') :: \mathrm{rest}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Parsing a single in-range entry]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_singleton}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_singleton}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux}
\difficulty{2}
Fix $w \ge 1$, and let $(\mathrm{idx}, \mathrm{dir})$ be a single entry whose index
satisfies $\mathrm{idx} < w$. Then parsing the one-element list $[(\mathrm{idx},
\mathrm{dir})]$ yields the singleton list $[(\mathrm{idx}, \mathrm{dir},
\mathrm{false})]$, where the index is viewed as an element of $\{0, 1, \dots, w-1\}$ and
the marker flag is $\mathrm{false}$ (there is no following entry to carry a termination
marker).
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Parsing the empty list]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_nil}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_nil}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux}
\difficulty{1}
Fix a positive width $w$. Parsing the empty aux list into triples yields the empty list
of triples.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Round-trip recovery of triple lists]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_triplesToAux}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_triplesToAux}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.parseAux, SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_cons_marker, SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_cons_nonmarker, SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_nil, SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_singleton, SwitchingLemma2.triplesToAux}
\difficulty{5}
Fix a width $w \ge 1$, and let $ts$ be any finite list of triples $(p, d, m)$, where the
position $p$ ranges over $\{0, 1, \dots, w-1\}$ and $d, m$ are Boolean flags. Converting
$ts$ into an aux list of index–direction entries — appending a termination marker, the
pair consisting of the out-of-range index $w$ together with the flag false, after each
triple whose flag $m$ is true — and then parsing that aux list back into triples
recovers exactly the original list $ts$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Triples-to-aux conversion distributes over concatenation]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.triplesToAux_append}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.triplesToAux_append}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.triplesToAux}
\difficulty{3}
Fix a width $w \in \bbn$, and let $\Phi$ denote the triples-to-aux conversion, which
turns a finite list of triples in $\mathrm{Fin}(w) \times \mathrm{Bool} \times
\mathrm{Bool}$ into an aux list of $(\bbn \times \mathrm{Bool})$ entries. Then $\Phi$
carries concatenation to concatenation: for any two such lists $T_1$ and $T_2$, \[
\Phi(T_1 \mathbin{+\!\!+} T_2) = \Phi(T_1) \mathbin{+\!\!+} \Phi(T_2). \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Length bound for processing a clause's literals]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_len_add}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_len_add}
\leanok
\uses{Literal, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\mathit{lits}$ be a list of literals on $n$ variables
each paired with its position index, let $\mathit{path}$ be a list of variable–direction
pairs, and let $\rho_0$ and $\sigma$ be restrictions on $n$ variables. Running the
clause-processing procedure on $\mathit{lits}$, $\mathit{path}$, $\rho_0$, and $\sigma$
yields, among its outputs, a remaining path and a list of accumulated auxiliary pairs.
The length of the auxiliary list plus the length of the remaining path is at most the
length of $\mathit{path}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Mark the last entry of a block]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.markLast}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.markLast}
\leanok
Builds a triple list from a $\mathrm{Fin}\,w \times \mathrm{Bool}$ block by
setting the marker flag to true on the last entry only and to false on all
others.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Round-trip of a marked block through the aux list]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.triplesToAux_markLast}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.triplesToAux_markLast}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.markLast, SwitchingLemma2.triplesToAux}
\difficulty{4}
Let $w \in \bbn$ and let $b$ be a nonempty list of pairs in $\mathrm{Fin}\,w \times
\mathrm{Bool}$. If one first marks the last entry of $b$ (setting the marker flag to
true on the final pair and false on all others) and then converts the resulting list of
triples back into an aux list, the outcome is the list obtained from $b$ by casting each
pair $(i, d)$ to the entry $(i, d) \in \bbn \times \mathrm{Bool}$, followed by the
single termination marker $(w, \mathrm{false})$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Marking preserves nonemptiness]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.markLast_ne_nil}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.markLast_ne_nil}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.markLast}
\difficulty{2}
Let $w$ be a natural number and let $\ell$ be a nonempty list of pairs in
$\mathrm{Fin}\,w \times \{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$. Then the marked list obtained
from $\ell$ by appending a boolean flag to each entry — true on the final entry and
false on every other — is again nonempty.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Last-entry marking preserves block length]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.markLast_length}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.markLast_length}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.markLast}
\difficulty{3}
Fix a width $w$, and let $B = ((i_1,b_1),\dots,(i_k,b_k))$ be a finite list whose
entries are pairs, each consisting of an index in $\{0,1,\dots,w-1\}$ together with a
boolean. Form a new list of triples by appending to every entry a marker flag, set to
true on the final entry of $B$ and to false on all earlier entries. Then this list of
triples has the same length as $B$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Last entry of a marked block carries the marker flag]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.markLast_getLast_true}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.markLast_getLast_true}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.markLast, SwitchingLemma2.markLast_ne_nil}
\difficulty{3}
Let $w$ be a natural number and let $b$ be a list of pairs in $\mathrm{Fin}\,w \times
\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}$, and suppose that its marked form — the list of
triples obtained by appending to each entry a marker flag that is $\mathrm{true}$ on the
final entry and $\mathrm{false}$ on every other — is nonempty. Then the marker flag of
the last triple of this marked list equals $\mathrm{true}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Cast an in-range aux list into Fin blocks]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock}
\leanok
Casts a list of $(\mathbb{N} \times \mathrm{Bool})$ entries, all of whose first
coordinates are $< w$, into a list of $(\mathrm{Fin}\,w \times \mathrm{Bool})$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Casting to bounded blocks preserves length]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock_length}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock_length}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock}
\difficulty{2}
Fix a natural number $w$ and let $l$ be a finite list of pairs $(i, b)$ with $i \in
\bbn$ and $b$ a Boolean, every first coordinate of which satisfies $i < w$. Recasting
$l$ into a list of pairs in $\mathrm{Fin}\,w \times \{\text{true}, \text{false}\}$ — by
reinterpreting each index $i$ as the element of $\mathrm{Fin}\,w$ it names, while
leaving the Booleans untouched — yields a list of the same length as $l$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Bounded-index cast is undone by taking values]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock_map}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock_map}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock}
\difficulty{2}
Fix a natural number $w$, and let $l$ be a finite list of pairs $(i,b)$ with $i \in
\bbn$ and $b$ a Boolean, subject to the requirement that $i < w$ for every pair in $l$.
Reinterpret each such pair as $(\bar\imath, b)$, where $\bar\imath$ is the element of
$\mathrm{Fin}\,w$ whose underlying value is $i$, obtaining a list over $\mathrm{Fin}\,w
\times \mathrm{Bool}$. Applying the map $(j,b) \mapsto (j\text{'s underlying natural
number}, b)$ to each entry of that list yields $l$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Nonemptiness of the Fin-block cast]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock_ne_nil}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock_ne_nil}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock}
\difficulty{2}
Fix $w \in \bbn$, and let $l$ be a list of pairs $(i, b) \in \bbn \times
\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ each of whose first coordinates satisfies $i < w$. If
$l$ is nonempty, then its cast into a list of pairs in $\mathrm{Fin}\,w \times
\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ is again nonempty.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Auxiliary indices bounded by term length]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_aux_idx_lt}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_aux_idx_lt}
\leanok
\uses{Literal, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_aux_entries_from_lits, Term}
\difficulty{3}
Let $t$ be a term on $n$ variables (a list of literals), and let $\ell$ be a list of
literal–index pairs with the property that every pair in $\ell$ occurs in the indexed
enumeration of $t$; that is, each entry of $\ell$ is a literal of $t$ paired with its
position in $t$. Then for any decision-tree path and any restrictions $\rho_0,\sigma$,
every pair $(i,b)$ appearing in the auxiliary output produced when $\ell$ is processed
against the path against $t$ satisfies $i < \lvert t\rvert$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Well-formedness invariant of the encoder's auxiliary output]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.encode_go_wellformed}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.encode_go_wellformed}
\leanok
\uses{DNF, DNF.width, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.freeVars, SwitchingLemma2.Term.killedBy, SwitchingLemma2.encode_go_acc, SwitchingLemma2.markLast, SwitchingLemma2.markLast_getLast_true, SwitchingLemma2.markLast_length, SwitchingLemma2.markLast_ne_nil, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_aux_idx_lt, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_len_add, SwitchingLemma2.term_length_le_width, SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock, SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock_length, SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock_map, SwitchingLemma2.toFinBlock_ne_nil, SwitchingLemma2.triplesToAux, SwitchingLemma2.triplesToAux_append, SwitchingLemma2.triplesToAux_markLast}
\difficulty{6}
Let $f$ be a DNF formula on $n$ variables whose width does not exceed a positive integer
$w$, and fix a recursion-budget (fuel) parameter, a path $P$ presented as a list of
variable–direction pairs in $\mathrm{Fin}\,n \times \mathrm{Bool}$, and two restrictions
$\rho_0$ and $\sigma$ on the $n$ variables. Run the Razborov encoder's recursive worker
on $f$, $w$, the fuel, $P$, $\rho_0$, and $\sigma$ starting from an empty auxiliary
accumulator, and let $A$ be its auxiliary output, a list of pairs in $\bbn \times
\mathrm{Bool}$. Then there exists a list $ts$ of triples in $\mathrm{Fin}\,w \times
\mathrm{Bool} \times \mathrm{Bool}$ such that $A$ is exactly the aux list obtained from
$ts$ by the triples-to-aux conversion, the number of triples in $ts$ is at most the
length of $P$, and, whenever $ts$ is nonempty, the marker flag (the final Boolean
component) of its last triple equals true.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Injectivity of the Razborov encoding on its auxiliary output]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.exists_aux_injection}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.exists_aux_injection}
\leanok
\proofsource{switching-lemma}{pdf-b5e074215b9e-p002-b004}
\uses{DNF, DNF.eval, DNF.width, DecisionTree.deepPath, SwitchingLemma2.IsBadRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree, SwitchingLemma2.encode_go_wellformed, SwitchingLemma2.parseAux, SwitchingLemma2.parseAux_triplesToAux, SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode, SwitchingLemma2.triplesToAux}
\difficulty{7}
Let $f$ be a DNF formula on $n$ variables whose width is at most $w$, let $w$ satisfy $w
> 0$, let $d$ be a natural number, and let $\gamma$ be a fixed restriction on the same
$n$ variables. Consider the collection of all restrictions $\rho$ that are bad for the
Boolean function computed by $f$ at depth $d$ — that is, the function $x \mapsto
f(\rho.\mathrm{extend}\,x)$ has decision-tree depth strictly greater than $d$ — and
whose Razborov encoding with parameters $w,d$ has first component equal to $\gamma$;
write $S$ for the set of auxiliary lists $\mathrm{aux} \in (\bbn \times
\mathrm{Bool})^{*}$ arising as the second component of the Razborov encoding of such a
$\rho$. Then there exists a map $g$ from auxiliary lists to functions $\mathrm{Fin}\,d
\to \mathrm{Fin}\,w \times \mathrm{Bool} \times \mathrm{Bool}$ that is injective on $S$.
\end{lemma}

\uses{DNF, DNF.eval, DNF.width, SwitchingLemma2.IsBadRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.exists_aux_injection, SwitchingLemma2.fixedTerm_implies_dtDepth_zero, SwitchingLemma2.killedAll_implies_dtDepth_zero, SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode, SwitchingLemma2.restrictFn, SwitchingLemma2.term_length_le_width, dtDepth}
\difficulty{5}
Let $f$ be a DNF formula on $n$ variables whose width is at most $w$, let $d$ be a
natural number, and let $\gamma$ be a fixed restriction. Write the Razborov encoding of
$f$ with parameters $w, d$ on a restriction $\rho$ as a pair $(\gamma_\rho,
\mathrm{aux}_\rho)$, where $\gamma_\rho$ is the extended restriction and
$\mathrm{aux}_\rho$ is the auxiliary list. Consider those restrictions $\rho$ that are
bad for the Boolean function computed by $f$ at depth $d$ — that is, the restriction of
that function by $\rho$ has decision-tree depth strictly greater than $d$ — and that
satisfy $\gamma_\rho = \gamma$. Then the number of distinct auxiliary lists
$\mathrm{aux}_\rho$ arising from such $\rho$ is at most $(4w)^d$.
\end{lemma}

\uses{DNF, DNF.eval, DNF.width, SwitchingLemma2.IsBadRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.IsRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.aux_image_card_bound, SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode, SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode_injective}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f$ be a DNF formula on $n$ variables whose width is at most $w$, and suppose no
variable occurs twice within any single term of $f$ (any two literals of a term sharing
a variable are equal). Fix natural numbers $s$ and $d$ with $d \le s$, and fix a target
restriction $\gamma$. Consider the restrictions $\rho$ that are *bad* — having exactly
$s$ free variables while the Boolean function $x \mapsto f(\rho.\mathrm{extend}\,x)$
computed by $f$ under $\rho$ has decision-tree depth strictly greater than $d$ — and
that the Razborov encoding sends to $\gamma$, i.e.\ the first component of the encoding
of $f$ and $\rho$ with parameters $w, d$ equals $\gamma$. The number of such
restrictions $\rho$ is at most $(4w)^d$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Count of restrictions with a fixed number of free variables]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.card_filter_numFree_eq}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.card_filter_numFree_eq}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.freeVars, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.numFree, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_path_length_eq}
\difficulty{6}
Fix natural numbers $n$ and $k$. Among all restrictions on $n$ variables — maps
assigning each index $i \in \mathrm{Fin}\,n$ either a fixed Boolean value or leaving it
free — the number of those having exactly $k$ free variables equals
$\binom{n}{k}\,2^{\,n-k}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Fixing a free variable reduces the free count by one]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.numFree_update_free}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.numFree_update_free}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.freeVars, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.numFree}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\rho$ be a restriction on $n$ variables, let $v$ be a variable that is free under
$\rho$, and let $b$ be a Boolean value. Let $\rho'$ be the restriction obtained from
$\rho$ by fixing $v$ to the value $b$ and leaving every other variable unchanged. Then
the number of free variables of $\rho'$ is one less than the number of free variables of
$\rho$; equivalently, if $f(\rho)$ denotes the number of free variables of $\rho$, then
\[
f(\rho') + 1 = f(\rho).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Preservation of free-variable agreement under clause processing]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_freeVars_agree}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_freeVars_agree}
\leanok
\uses{Literal, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits}
\difficulty{4}
Fix a list of literals with position indices and a decision-tree path, and let $\rho_0$
and $\sigma$ be two restrictions on $n$ variables that agree on which variables are
free: for every variable $v$, $\rho_0(v)$ is free if and only if $\sigma(v)$ is free.
Let $\rho_0'$ and $\sigma'$ be the updated restrictions produced by processing the
clause's literals against the path starting from $\rho_0$ and $\sigma$. Then $\rho_0'$
and $\sigma'$ again agree on their free variables: for every $v$, $\rho_0'(v)$ is free
if and only if $\sigma'(v)$ is free.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Free-variable count of the σ-output after processing a clause]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_numFree_σ}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_numFree_σ}
\leanok
\uses{Literal, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.numFree, SwitchingLemma2.numFree_update_free, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits}
\difficulty{5}
Fix a list of literals on $n$ variables, each paired with its position index within its
clause; a decision path presented as a list of variable–direction pairs; and two
restrictions $\rho_0, \sigma$ on $n$ variables. For a restriction $\rho$, write
$F(\rho)$ for the number of variables left free by $\rho$. Suppose that $\rho_0$ and
$\sigma$ are free at exactly the same variables (for every variable $v$, $\rho_0(v)$ is
unset if and only if $\sigma(v)$ is unset), that each listed literal's variable is free
in $\rho_0$, and that the listed literals have pairwise distinct variables. Let
$\sigma'$ be the restriction returned as the $\sigma$-component of processing these
literals against the path. Then
\[
F(\sigma') + \min(\ell, m) = F(\sigma),
\]
where $\ell$ is the number of literals and $m$ is the length of the path.
\end{lemma}

Let $f$ be a DNF formula on $n$ Boolean variables, let $\rho$ be a restriction of those
variables, and let $d$ be a natural number. Write $f|_\rho$ for the restricted Boolean
function, which sends an assignment $x$ to the value of $f$ on the assignment that
agrees with $\rho$ on its fixed variables and with $x$ on its free variables. Suppose
$\rho$ is bad for $f$ at depth $d$, meaning that the decision-tree depth of $f|_\rho$ —
the least depth of any decision tree computing $f|_\rho$ — is strictly greater than $d$.
Then the deepest root-to-leaf path of the canonical decision tree of $f$ under $\rho$
has length strictly greater than $d$.
\end{lemma}

Let $f$ be a DNF formula on $n$ variables, let $\rho$ be a restriction of those
variables, and let $d$ be a natural number. Suppose $\rho$ is bad for $f$ at depth $d$:
the restriction $x \mapsto f(\rho.\mathrm{extend}\,x)$ of the Boolean function computed
by $f$ has decision-tree depth strictly greater than $d$. Then the deepest root-to-leaf
path of the canonical decision tree of $f$ under $\rho$, truncated to its first $d$
steps, is a sequence of exactly $d$ pairs (queried variable, branch direction) —
equivalently, that path has length at least $d$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Path length consumed by clause processing]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_path_length_eq}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_path_length_eq}
\leanok
\uses{Literal, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits}
\difficulty{3}
Run the clause-processing operation on a list of literals — each tagged with its
position in the clause — and a decision-tree path (a list of variable–direction pairs),
starting from restrictions $\rho_0$ and $\sigma$. Writing $\ell$ for the number of
literals and $m$ for the length of the path, the residual path returned by the operation
has length exactly $m - \min(\ell, m)$; equivalently, this residual length together with
$\min(\ell, m)$ sums to $m$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Fixing a variable lowers the free count by at most one]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.numFree_update_some_ge}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.numFree_update_some_ge}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.freeVars, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.numFree, SwitchingLemma2.numFree_update_free}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\rho$ be a restriction on $n$ variables, let $v$ be one of these variables, and let
$b$ be a Boolean value. Let $\rho'$ be the restriction that fixes $v$ to $b$ and agrees
with $\rho$ on every other variable. Writing $f(\sigma)$ for the number of free
variables of a restriction $\sigma$, we have $f(\rho') + 1 \ge f(\rho)$; that is, fixing
a single variable reduces the number of free variables by at most one.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Free-variable bound on the leftover path]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_remaining_le_numFree}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_remaining_le_numFree}
\leanok
\uses{Literal, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.numFree, SwitchingLemma2.numFree_update_some_ge, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\rho_0$ and $\sigma$ be restrictions on $n$ variables, let $L$ be a list of
literals each paired with its position index in a clause, and let $P$ be a decision-tree
path (a list of variable–direction pairs). Suppose the length of $P$ is at most the
number of free variables of $\rho_0$. Write $(P', \rho_0', \sigma', A)$ for the result
of processing $L$ against $P$ starting from $\rho_0$ and $\sigma$, so that $P'$ is the
remaining path and $\rho_0'$ the updated first restriction. Then the length of $P'$ is
at most the number of free variables of $\rho_0'$.
\end{lemma}

tree for $f|_\rho$ has depth $0$.
\end{lemma}

\difficulty{3}
Let $f$ be a DNF formula on $n$ Boolean variables and let $\rho$ be a restriction on
those variables. If some term of $f$ is fixed by $\rho$ — that is, at least one
conjunction of literals in $f$ has every literal fixed to true by $\rho$ — then the
canonical decision tree of $f$ under $\rho$ has depth $0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Canonical path predicate]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.IsCanonicalPath}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.IsCanonicalPath}
\leanok
\statementsource{switching-lemma}{
  pdf-b5e074215b9e-p002-b002,
  pdf-b5e074215b9e-p002-b003
}
\uses{DNF, DecisionTree.deepPath, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree}
$\mathrm{IsCanonicalPath}\,f\,\rho\,\mathrm{path}$ holds when $\mathrm{path}$ is an
initial segment of the canonical decision tree's deepest root-to-leaf path for
$f|_\rho$, i.e.\ $\mathrm{path} = (\mathrm{canonicalDTree}\,f\,\rho).\mathrm{deepPath}.\mathrm{take}\,(\mathrm{path.length})$.
This is the invariant carried by the Razborov encoder.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Indexing a term preserves the count of matching literals]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.zipIdx_filter_length}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.zipIdx_filter_length}
\leanok
\uses{Literal, Term}
\difficulty{2}
Let $t$ be a term over $n$ variables, that is, a finite list of literals, and let $p$ be
a predicate on literals. Form from $t$ the indexed list in which each literal is paired
with its position in $t$. Then the number of entries of this indexed list whose literal
component satisfies $p$ equals the number of literals of $t$ that satisfy $p$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Filtering commutes with position annotation on literals]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.zipIdx_filter_getElem_fst}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.zipIdx_filter_getElem_fst}
\leanok
\uses{Literal, Term}
\difficulty{3}
Let $t = (\ell_0,\ell_1,\dots,\ell_{m-1})$ be a term, that is a list of literals over
$\mathrm{Fin}\,n$, and let $p$ be a Boolean predicate on literals. Annotate each literal
with its position to obtain the list of pairs $(\ell_i, i)$, and retain those pairs
whose literal satisfies $p$; separately, retain the literals of $t$ that satisfy $p$.
Then for every index $k$ that is smaller than the length of both retained lists, the
literal in the $k$-th retained pair equals the $k$-th retained literal of $t$.
\end{lemma}

\uses{DNF, DecisionTree, DecisionTree.deepPath, DecisionTree.depth, Literal, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.freeVars, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.numFree, SwitchingLemma2.Term.fixedBy, SwitchingLemma2.Term.killedBy, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree_alive_eq_termSubTree', SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree_depth_zero_of_fixed, SwitchingLemma2.termSubTree_deepPath_var_match, SwitchingLemma2.zipIdx_filter_getElem_fst, SwitchingLemma2.zipIdx_filter_length, Term}
\difficulty{5}
Let $f$ be a DNF formula on $n$ Boolean variables and $\rho$ a restriction, and let $t$
be the first term of $f$, in list order, that is not killed by $\rho$. Suppose the
literals of $t$ are pairwise distinct and no two of them share a variable, and write
$l_{i_0}, l_{i_1}, \ldots$ for the subsequence of literals of $t$ whose variables are
free under $\rho$, taken in their order of occurrence in $t$. Then for every index $k$
smaller than both the number of these free literals and the length of the deepest
root-to-leaf path of the canonical decision tree of $f$ under $\rho$, the variable
queried at the $k$-th step of that path equals the variable of the $k$-th free literal
$l_{i_k}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[The remaining path is a suffix of the input path]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_fst_eq_drop}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_fst_eq_drop}
\leanok
\uses{Literal, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\ell$ be a list of free literals of a clause, each paired with its position index,
and let $p$ be a decision-tree path, that is, a list of variable–direction pairs; let
$\rho_0$ and $\sigma$ be restrictions on $n$ variables. Then the remaining path returned
by processing $\ell$ against $p$ (starting from $\rho_0$ and $\sigma$) is exactly the
suffix of $p$ obtained by deleting its first $\min(|\ell|,\,|p|)$ entries.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Free variables removed when processing a clause]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_numFree_ρ_eq}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_numFree_ρ_eq}
\leanok
\uses{Literal, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.numFree, SwitchingLemma2.numFree_update_free, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\rho_0$ and $\sigma$ be restrictions on $n$ variables, and write $f(\rho)$ for the
number of free variables of a restriction $\rho$. Present a single clause as a list of
$k$ literals, each paired with its position index, and a decision-tree path as a list of
$m$ variable–direction pairs. Suppose that every literal's variable is free in $\rho_0$
and that the listed literals have pairwise distinct variables. Let $\rho_0'$ be the
updated restriction returned in place of $\rho_0$ when these literals are processed
against the path. Then
\[
f(\rho_0') + \min(k, m) = f(\rho_0),
\]
so processing fixes exactly $\min(k, m)$ of the previously free variables of $\rho_0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Deepest path after dropping the free-literal prefix]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_termSubTree_drop}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_termSubTree_drop}
\leanok
\uses{DecisionTree, DecisionTree.deepPath, Literal, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.freeVars, SwitchingLemma2.filter_free_update_eq, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits, SwitchingLemma2.termSubTree, SwitchingLemma2.termSubTree_cons_nonfree, SwitchingLemma2.termSubTree_deepPath_head_free, Term}
\difficulty{6}
Let $t$ be a term on $n$ variables whose literals have pairwise distinct variables, let
$\rho_0$ and $\sigma$ be restrictions on $n$ variables, and let $c$ be a continuation
sending each restriction to a decision tree. Let $S$ be the sub-tree built for $t$ under
$\rho_0$ with continuation $c$, and let $\pi$ denote its deepest root-to-leaf path.
Write $F$ for the sublist of $t$ consisting of those literals whose variable is free
under $\rho_0$, and set $m = |F|$. Suppose $L$ is a list of $m$ literal–index pairs
whose literal components are exactly $F$, in order, and that $P$ is a list of
variable–direction pairs coinciding with the length-$|P|$ prefix of $\pi$, with $m \le
|P| \le |\pi|$. Then dropping the first $m$ entries of $\pi$ leaves exactly the deepest
path of $c$ evaluated at the restriction obtained from $\rho_0$ and $\sigma$ by
processing the literals $L$ against the path $P$ (the updated $\rho_0$ component that
this process returns).
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Clause processing preserves the canonical path]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.canonicalPath_preserve_processClauseLits}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.canonicalPath_preserve_processClauseLits}
\leanok
\uses{DNF, DecisionTree.deepPath, DecisionTree.depth, DecisionTree.length_deepPath, Literal, SwitchingLemma2.IsCanonicalPath, SwitchingLemma2.Literal.fixedBy, SwitchingLemma2.Literal.killedBy, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.freeVars, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.numFree, SwitchingLemma2.Term.fixedBy, SwitchingLemma2.Term.killedBy, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree_alive_eq_termSubTree', SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree_depth_zero_of_fixed, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree_depth_zero_of_killed, SwitchingLemma2.cont_eq_canonicalDTree, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_fst_eq_drop, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_numFree_ρ_eq, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_termSubTree_drop, SwitchingLemma2.termSubTree, SwitchingLemma2.zipIdx_filter_getElem_fst, SwitchingLemma2.zipIdx_filter_length, Term}
\difficulty{7}
Fix $n$, a DNF formula $f$ on $n$ variables, and two restrictions $\rho_0$ and $\sigma$
on those variables. Suppose $t$ is the first term of $f$ not killed by $\rho_0$, that
$t$ has no repeated literal, and that any two literals of $t$ with equal variables are
themselves equal. Let $\mathrm{lits}$ be the list of literals of $t$ whose variable is
free under $\rho_0$, each tagged with its position in $t$, and let $\mathrm{path}$ be a
canonical path for $f|_{\rho_0}$ — an initial segment of the deepest root-to-leaf path
of the canonical decision tree of $f|_{\rho_0}$ — of length at most the depth of the
canonical decision tree of $f|_{\rho_0}$. Assume that for every index $k$ below the
smaller of the lengths of $\mathrm{lits}$ and $\mathrm{path}$, the variable of the
$k$-th literal of $\mathrm{lits}$ equals the variable queried at the $k$-th step of
$\mathrm{path}$. Process $\mathrm{lits}$ against $\mathrm{path}$ in lockstep, one path
step per literal, forming a restriction $\rho_0'$ and a shortened path $\mathrm{path}'$
as follows: a literal with variable $v$ and negation flag $b$ aligned with a path step
of direction $d$ contributes the assignment $v \mapsto d$ to $\rho_0'$ (and the
assignment $v \mapsto \lnot b$ to $\sigma$), and its path step is dropped; $\rho_0'$
agrees with $\rho_0$ on every other variable, and $\mathrm{path}'$ is the unconsumed
tail of $\mathrm{path}$. Then $\mathrm{path}'$ is a canonical path for $f|_{\rho_0'}$,
and the length of $\mathrm{path}'$ is at most the depth of the canonical decision tree
of $f|_{\rho_0'}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Free literals of a term have pairwise distinct variables]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_freeLits_pairwise_var}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_freeLits_pairwise_var}
\leanok
\uses{Literal, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.freeVars, Term}
\difficulty{4}
Let $t$ be a term on $n$ variables (a list of literals) and let $\rho$ be a restriction
on those variables. Suppose that $t$ contains no repeated literal, and that any two
literals of $t$ sharing the same underlying variable are in fact equal. Form the list of
literals of $t$ whose variable is free under $\rho$, each kept together with its
position in $t$. Then this list has pairwise distinct variables: any two of its entries
carry different variables.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Free-variable consumption invariant of the Razborov encoder]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode_go_numFree_invariant}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode_go_numFree_invariant}
\leanok
\uses{DNF, DecisionTree.deepPath, DecisionTree.depth, DecisionTree.length_deepPath, Literal, SwitchingLemma2.IsCanonicalPath, SwitchingLemma2.Literal.killedBy, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.freeVars, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.numFree, SwitchingLemma2.Term.fixedBy, SwitchingLemma2.Term.killedBy, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree_deepPath_match_freeLits, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree_depth_zero_of_fixed, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree_depth_zero_of_killed, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalPath_preserve_processClauseLits, SwitchingLemma2.choose_mul_pow_bound, SwitchingLemma2.encode_go_acc, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_freeLits_pairwise_var, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_freeVars_agree, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_len_add, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_numFree_σ, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_path_le, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_path_length_eq}
\difficulty{7}
Let $f$ be a DNF formula on $n$ Boolean variables in which, within each term, any two
literals on the same variable are equal and no literal occurs more than once, and fix an
arbitrary width $w \in \bbn$. Let $\rho_0$ and $\sigma$ be restrictions on these $n$
variables that leave exactly the same variables free (for every variable $v$,
$\rho_0(v)$ is unset iff $\sigma(v)$ is), and let $\mathrm{path}$ be a prefix of the
deepest root-to-leaf path of the canonical decision tree for $f|_{\rho_0}$, of length at
most the depth of that tree. If the fuel parameter strictly exceeds the length of
$\mathrm{path}$, then the restriction returned by the Razborov encoder run on $f$ with
width $w$, this fuel, $\mathrm{path}$, $\rho_0$, and $\sigma$ has exactly
$\lvert\mathrm{path}\rvert$ fewer free variables than $\sigma$; that is, its number of
free variables plus $\lvert\mathrm{path}\rvert$ equals the number of free variables of
$\sigma$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Free-variable count of the Razborov encoding's output]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode_fst_numFree_eq}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode_fst_numFree_eq}
\leanok

\uses{DNF, DNF.eval, DecisionTree.deepPath, DecisionTree.depth, SwitchingLemma2.IsBadRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.IsCanonicalPath, SwitchingLemma2.IsRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.numFree, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree, SwitchingLemma2.canonicalDTree_depth_ge, SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode, SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode_go_numFree_invariant, SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode_path_length, SwitchingLemma2.restrictFn, dtDepth}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f$ be a DNF formula on $n$ Boolean variables in which no term repeats a literal,
and within each term any two literals on the same variable coincide (so each variable
occurs at most once per term). Let $\rho$ be a restriction with exactly $s$ free
variables, and let $w$ and $d$ be natural numbers with $d \le s$. Suppose $\rho$ is bad
for $f$ at depth $d$, meaning the restricted Boolean function $f|_\rho$ has
decision-tree depth strictly greater than $d$. Then the restriction forming the first
component of the Razborov encoding of $f$ and $\rho$ with parameters $w$ and $d$ has
exactly $s - d$ free variables.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Counting bound for bad restrictions of a DNF]

\uses{DNF, DNF.eval, DNF.width, SwitchingLemma2.IsBadRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.IsRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.numFree, SwitchingLemma2.card_filter_numFree_eq, SwitchingLemma2.fiber_bound, SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode, SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode_fst_numFree_eq}
\difficulty{5}
Let $f$ be a DNF formula on $n$ Boolean variables in which no two literals of the same
term share a variable and no term lists the same literal twice, and suppose every term
of $f$ has at most $w$ literals. Fix natural numbers $d \le s$. Then the number of
restrictions of the $n$ variables that leave exactly $s$ variables free and are bad for
$f$ at depth $d$ — that is, for which the restricted function $x \mapsto
f(\rho.\mathrm{extend}\,x)$ has decision-tree depth strictly greater than $d$ — is at
most
\[
\binom{n}{\,s-d\,}\, 2^{\,n-(s-d)}\, (4w)^{d}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[No bad restrictions with few free variables]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.bad_filter_empty_of_d_ge_s}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.bad_filter_empty_of_d_ge_s}
\leanok
\uses{DNF, DNF.eval, SwitchingLemma2.IsBadRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.IsRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.dtDepth_restrictFn_le_numFree}
\difficulty{2}
Let $f$ be a DNF formula in $n$ variables, and let $d$ and $s$ be natural numbers with
$s \le d$. Then no restriction of the $n$ variables that leaves exactly $s$ variables
free is bad for the Boolean function computed by $f$ at depth $d$; that is, the set of
restrictions $\rho$ that both have exactly $s$ free variables and whose restricted
function $x \mapsto f(\rho.\mathrm{extend}\,x)$ has decision-tree depth strictly greater
than $d$ is empty.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Decision tree to DNF]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.toDNF}
\statementsource{boolean-ch04-dnf-switching-lmn}{
  pdf-fc447f326910-p002-b006,
  pdf-fc447f326910-p002-b007
}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.toDNF}
\leanok
\statementsource{switching-lemma}{pdf-b5e074215b9e-p003-b003}
\uses{DNF, DecisionTree}
Converts a decision tree into a DNF whose terms are the conjunctions of literals
along each root-to-leaf path ending in a $\mathrm{true}$ leaf.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Decision tree to CNF]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.toCNF}
\statementsource{boolean-ch04-dnf-switching-lmn}{
  pdf-fc447f326910-p002-b006,
  pdf-fc447f326910-p002-b007
}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.toCNF}
\leanok
\statementsource{switching-lemma}{pdf-b5e074215b9e-p003-b003}
\uses{CNF, DecisionTree}
Converts a decision tree into a CNF whose clauses are the disjunctions of negated
literals along each root-to-leaf path ending in a $\mathrm{false}$ leaf.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Attainment of the decision-tree depth]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.dtDepth_witness}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.dtDepth_witness}
\leanok
\uses{DecisionTree, DecisionTree.depth, DecisionTree.eval, buildFullDTree, buildFullDTree_depth, buildFullDTree_eval, dtDepth}
\difficulty{3}
Let $f \colon (\mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \mathrm{Bool}) \to \mathrm{Bool}$ be a Boolean
function on $n$ variables, and let $d$ be its decision-tree depth. Then there exists a
decision tree $T$ of depth at most $d$ that computes $f$, meaning $T$ evaluated at $x$
equals $f(x)$ for every input $x$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Small decision-tree depth yields narrow DNF and CNF]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.dtDepth_le_implies_small_dnf_cnf}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.dtDepth_le_implies_small_dnf_cnf}
\leanok

\uses{CNF, CNF.eval, CNF.evalClause, CNF.width, DNF, DNF.eval, DNF.width, DecisionTree, DecisionTree.depth, DecisionTree.eval, Literal.eval, SwitchingLemma2.dtDepth_witness, SwitchingLemma2.toCNF, SwitchingLemma2.toDNF, Term.eval, dtDepth}
\difficulty{6}
Let $f : (\mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \bbf_2) \to \{0,1\}$ be a Boolean function, and let $d$ be
a natural number such that the decision-tree depth of $f$ is at most $d$. Then $f$ is
computed by a DNF formula of width at most $d$ and by a CNF formula of width at most
$d$; that is, there exist a disjunction of terms and a conjunction of clauses, each term
or clause containing at most $d$ literals, that both agree with $f$ on every input.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Flip a literal's polarity]
\lean{Literal.flipNeg}
\label{Literal.flipNeg}
\leanok
\uses{Literal}
Negates a literal by flipping its polarity bit while keeping its variable.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Flipping a literal negates its value]
\lean{Literal.flipNeg_eval}
\label{Literal.flipNeg_eval}
\leanok
\uses{Literal, Literal.eval, Literal.flipNeg}
\difficulty{2}
Let $l$ be a literal over $n$ Boolean variables, given by a variable index and a
polarity that marks it as positive or negated, and let $x \in
\{\text{true},\text{false}\}^n$ be an assignment. Writing $\bar{l}$ for the literal
obtained from $l$ by flipping its polarity while keeping the same variable, the value of
$\bar{l}$ under $x$ is the negation of the value of $l$ under $x$; that is, $\bar{l}(x)
= \lnot\, l(x)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Polarity flip preserves the underlying variable]
\lean{Literal.flipNeg_var}
\label{Literal.flipNeg_var}
\leanok
\uses{Literal, Literal.flipNeg}
\difficulty{1}
Let $l$ be a literal on $n$ variables, that is, a variable $v \in \{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$
together with a polarity bit. The literal obtained from $l$ by flipping its polarity has
the same underlying variable $v$ as $l$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Injectivity of literal polarity flipping]
\lean{Literal.flipNeg_injective}
\label{Literal.flipNeg_injective}
\leanok
\uses{Literal.flipNeg}
\difficulty{2}
Fix $n \in \bbn$, and recall that a literal is a pair consisting of a variable in $\{0,
1, \dots, n-1\}$ together with a polarity bit, and that flipping a literal's polarity
toggles this bit while leaving the variable unchanged. Then the polarity-flipping
operation is injective: if two literals have the same polarity flip, they are equal.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[CNF to De Morgan dual DNF]
\lean{cnfToDualDNF}
\label{cnfToDualDNF}
\leanok
\uses{CNF, DNF, Literal.flipNeg}
Converts a CNF $\psi$ to its De Morgan dual DNF by negating every literal, so each
clause (a disjunction) becomes a term (a conjunction) of negated literals:
$\lnot\bigl(\bigwedge_i \bigvee_j l_{ij}\bigr) = \bigvee_i \bigl(\bigwedge_j \lnot l_{ij}\bigr)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Width is preserved under De Morgan dualization]
\lean{cnfToDualDNF_width}
\label{cnfToDualDNF_width}
\leanok
\uses{CNF, CNF.width, DNF.width, Term.width, cnfToDualDNF}
\difficulty{2}
Let $\psi$ be a CNF formula over $n$ variables, and let $\psi^{*}$ be its De Morgan dual
DNF, obtained by negating every literal so that each clause becomes a term. Then
$\psi^{*}$ and $\psi$ have the same width; that is, the maximum term-length of
$\psi^{*}$ equals the maximum clause-width of $\psi$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[De Morgan dual of a CNF computes its negation]
\lean{cnfToDualDNF_eval}
\label{cnfToDualDNF_eval}
\leanok
\statementsource{boolean-ch04-dnf-switching-lmn}{pdf-fc447f326910-p002-b005}
\uses{CNF, CNF.eval, CNF.evalClause, DNF.eval, Literal.flipNeg_eval, Term.eval, cnfToDualDNF}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\psi$ be a formula in conjunctive normal form over $n$ Boolean variables — a
conjunction of clauses, each clause a disjunction of literals — and let its De Morgan
dual DNF be obtained by negating every literal of $\psi$, so that each clause $\bigvee_j
l_{ij}$ becomes the term $\bigwedge_j \lnot l_{ij}$. Then for every assignment $x \colon
\{0,\dots,n-1\} \to \{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}$, evaluating this dual DNF at $x$
yields exactly the negation of the value of $\psi$ at $x$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Negate decision tree leaves]
\lean{DecisionTree.negateLeaves}
\label{DecisionTree.negateLeaves}
\leanok
\uses{DecisionTree}
Negates every leaf of a decision tree, leaving its branching structure unchanged.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Negating leaves negates the evaluation]
\lean{DecisionTree.negateLeaves_eval}
\label{DecisionTree.negateLeaves_eval}
\leanok
\uses{DecisionTree, DecisionTree.eval, DecisionTree.negateLeaves}
\difficulty{3}
Let $T$ be a decision tree on $n$ Boolean variables, and let $x \colon \{0,\dots,n-1\}
\to \{\mathtt{false},\mathtt{true}\}$ be an assignment of the variables. Then the tree
obtained from $T$ by negating every leaf value evaluates on $x$ to the negation of the
value of $T$ on $x$; that is, its output equals $\lnot\,(T(x))$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Negating leaves preserves decision-tree depth]
\lean{DecisionTree.negateLeaves_depth}
\label{DecisionTree.negateLeaves_depth}
\leanok
\uses{DecisionTree, DecisionTree.depth, DecisionTree.negateLeaves}
\difficulty{2}
Let $T$ be a decision tree on $n$ Boolean variables, and let $T'$ be the tree obtained
from $T$ by negating the Boolean value at every leaf while leaving its branching
structure unchanged. Then $T'$ has the same depth as $T$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Decision-tree depth is invariant under negation]
\lean{dtDepth_neg}
\label{dtDepth_neg}
\leanok
\uses{DecisionTree, DecisionTree.depth, DecisionTree.eval, DecisionTree.negateLeaves, buildFullDTree, buildFullDTree_depth, buildFullDTree_eval, dtDepth}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f$ be a Boolean function on $n$ variables, and let $\bar f$ denote its pointwise
negation, so that $\bar f(x) = 1 - f(x)$ for every input $x$. Then $f$ and $\bar f$ have
the same decision-tree depth: $\operatorname{depth}_{\mathrm{DT}}(\bar f) =
\operatorname{depth}_{\mathrm{DT}}(f)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Restriction commutes with negation]
\lean{SwitchingLemmaCNF.restrictFn_neg}
\label{SwitchingLemmaCNF.restrictFn_neg}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.restrictFn}
\difficulty{1}
Let $f : (\mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \bbf_2) \to \bbf_2$ be a Boolean function and $\rho$ a
restriction on $n$ variables. Then restricting the negation of $f$ agrees, at every
point $x$, with the negation of the restriction of $f$; that is, $(\lnot f)$ restricted
by $\rho$ equals the pointwise negation of $f$ restricted by $\rho$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Negation-invariance of bad restrictions]
\lean{SwitchingLemmaCNF.IsBadRestriction_neg}
\label{SwitchingLemmaCNF.IsBadRestriction_neg}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.IsBadRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemmaCNF.restrictFn_neg, dtDepth_neg}
\difficulty{1}
Let $f : (\mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \mathrm{Bool}) \to \mathrm{Bool}$ be a Boolean function,
$d$ a natural number, and $\rho$ a restriction on the $n$ variables. Then $\rho$ is bad
for the negation $\lnot f$ at depth $d$ if and only if $\rho$ is bad for $f$ at depth
$d$; that is, the restricted function of $\lnot f$ under $\rho$ has decision-tree depth
greater than $d$ exactly when the restricted function of $f$ under $\rho$ does.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Dual DNF preserves duplicate-free clauses]
\lean{SwitchingLemmaCNF.cnfToDualDNF_nodup}
\label{SwitchingLemmaCNF.cnfToDualDNF_nodup}
\leanok
\uses{CNF, Literal.flipNeg_injective, cnfToDualDNF}
\difficulty{2}
Let $\psi$ be a CNF formula whose clauses are lists of literals, and suppose that every
clause of $\psi$ contains no repeated literal. Then every term of the De Morgan dual DNF
obtained from $\psi$ — the DNF formed by negating each literal of each clause — likewise
contains no repeated literal.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Dual DNF preserves within-clause variable-distinctness]
\lean{SwitchingLemmaCNF.cnfToDualDNF_inj}
\label{SwitchingLemmaCNF.cnfToDualDNF_inj}
\leanok
\uses{CNF, Literal.flipNeg_var, cnfToDualDNF}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\psi$ be a CNF formula on $n$ variables with the property that, within each of its
clauses, any two literals having the same variable are in fact the same literal (so no
variable occurs in a clause with both polarities, nor is any literal repeated). Then the
De Morgan dual DNF obtained from $\psi$ by negating every literal has the same property
term by term: within each of its terms, any two literals sharing a variable are equal.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Håstad's switching lemma for CNF formulas]
\lean{SwitchingLemmaCNF.switching_lemma_cnf}
\label{SwitchingLemmaCNF.switching_lemma_cnf}
\leanok

  {SwitchingLemmaCNF.cnfToDualDNF_inj}

  {pdf-b5e074215b9e-p003-b003}
\uses{CNF, CNF.eval, CNF.width, DNF.eval, DNF.width, SwitchingLemma2.IsBadRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.IsRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.numSRestrictions, SwitchingLemma2.switching_lemma, SwitchingLemmaCNF.cnfToDualDNF_inj, SwitchingLemmaCNF.cnfToDualDNF_nodup, SwitchingLemmaCNF.restrictFn_neg, cnfToDualDNF, cnfToDualDNF_eval, cnfToDualDNF_width, dtDepth_neg}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\psi$ be a CNF formula on $n \ge 1$ Boolean variables whose width is at most $w$,
and suppose that within each clause no literal is repeated and any two literals on the
same variable coincide, so that the literals of every clause lie on distinct variables.
Let $s$ and $d$ be natural numbers with $5s \le n$. For a restriction $\rho$ leaving
some variables free and fixing the rest, write $\psi\!\restriction_\rho$ for the Boolean
function $x \mapsto \psi\bigl(\rho.\mathrm{extend}\,x\bigr)$ obtained by evaluating
$\psi$ with the fixed coordinates set by $\rho$ and the free coordinates supplied by
$x$, and let $\mathrm{depth}(\psi\!\restriction_\rho)$ denote its decision-tree depth,
the least depth of a decision tree computing it. Then, counting restrictions that leave
exactly $s$ variables free and under which the restricted function still requires depth
greater than $d$,
\[
\bigl|\{\rho : \rho \text{ leaves exactly } s \text{ variables free and }
\mathrm{depth}(\psi\!\restriction_\rho) > d\}\bigr| \cdot n^{d}
  \;\le\; \binom{n}{s}\, 2^{\,n-s}\,(10\,s\,w)^{d}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Switching lemma corollary for CNF formulas]
\lean{SwitchingLemmaCNF.switching_corollary_cnf}
\proofsource{switching-lemma}{pdf-b5e074215b9e-p003-b004}
\label{SwitchingLemmaCNF.switching_corollary_cnf}
\leanok
\statementsource{switching-lemma}{pdf-b5e074215b9e-p003-b004}
\statementsource{boolean-ch04-dnf-switching-lmn}{pdf-fc447f326910-p008-b005}
\uses{CNF, CNF.eval, CNF.width, DNF, DNF.eval, DNF.width, SwitchingLemma2.IsRestriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.dtDepth_le_implies_small_dnf_cnf, SwitchingLemma2.numSRestrictions, SwitchingLemma2.restrictFn, SwitchingLemmaCNF.switching_lemma_cnf, dtDepth}
\difficulty{4}
Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\psi$ be a CNF formula on $n$ Boolean variables whose width is at
most $w$, meaning every clause of $\psi$ has at most $w$ literals; assume moreover that
no clause of $\psi$ repeats a literal or uses a variable in two of its literals, and
that $5s \le n$. Call a restriction $\rho$ that leaves exactly $s$ of the $n$ variables
free \emph{bad} if the restricted function $x \mapsto \psi(\rho.\mathrm{extend}\,x)$ is
computed by no DNF formula of width at most $w$. Then the number $B$ of bad restrictions
satisfies
\[
  B \cdot n^{w} \;\le\; \binom{n}{s}\, 2^{\,n-s} \, (10\,s\,w)^{w}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\section{Additional declarations}

\begin{lemma}[A binomial coefficient and power inequality]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.choose_mul_pow_bound}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.choose_mul_pow_bound}
\leanok
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$, $s$, and $d$ be natural numbers satisfying $5s \le n$ and $d \le s$. Then
\[
  \binom{n}{s-d}\,(4n)^d \;\le\; \binom{n}{s}\,(5s)^d .
\]
\end{lemma}
